title: Verb Wise: North American Expressions Collection
description: Standalone data conversion of the document "Verb Wise: North American Expressions Collection": 25 American and 25 Canadian English expressions with Spanish (Spain) equivalents, English meanings, example sentences, verification statuses and explanatory notes.

american.meaning: wry, strong agreement
american.verificationNote: Attested: RAE Diccionario del estudiante (decir, coloq.), “Se usa para expresar conformidad o acuerdo”; SpanishDict. “A mí me lo vas a contar” dropped: no source found for that sense
american.exampleEnglish: Tell me about it, Madrid rents are insane.
american.exampleSpanish: Y que lo digas, los alquileres en Madrid son una locura.

american.meaning: ironic disbelief
american.verificationNote: Attested: WordReference (¡venga!, disbelief, informal); SpanishDict (anda ya). “Sí, hombre” can also mean “of course”, so tone matters. “Ya, ya” found in no source
american.exampleEnglish: Yeah, right, he’ll pay you back.
american.exampleSpanish: Sí, hombre, como si te fuera a devolver el dinero.

american.meaning: an exasperated "come on!": stop annoying me, or I don't believe that
american.verificationNote: Attested for the “oh, come on” sense: The Local Spain, WordReference. No source covers the “cut me some slack” sense
american.exampleEnglish: Give me a break, you were late again!
american.exampleSpanish: ¡Venga ya, otra vez llegas tarde!

american.meaning: get straight to the main point, skipping the preamble
american.verificationNote: Attested: WordReference (loc. verb, informal), Wiktionary. The DLE page for grano would not load
american.exampleEnglish: Let’s cut to the chase.
american.exampleSpanish: Vayamos al grano.

american.meaning: avoid the main point by talking around it, usually out of reluctance
american.spanish: Andarse por las ramas / andar con rodeos
american.verificationNote: Attested: SpanishDict, WordReference. SpanishDict also lists marear la perdiz (Spain). The DLE page for rama would not load
american.exampleEnglish: Stop beating around the bush.
american.exampleSpanish: Deja de andarte por las ramas.

american.english: Hit the nail on the head
american.meaning: say or do exactly the right thing; be precisely right
american.verificationNote: DLE: clavo, loc. verb. coloq., “Acertar en lo que se hace o dice”
american.exampleEnglish: You hit the nail on the head about the rent.
american.exampleSpanish: Diste en el clavo con lo del alquiler.

american.meaning: an obvious major problem that everyone avoids mentioning
american.spanish: El elefante en la habitación (formal: el tema tabú)
american.verificationNote: Attested in Spain’s press: Público, elDiario.es (“esa cuestión obvia cuyo debate se evita”). A calque; no dictionary entry found
american.exampleEnglish: Nobody mentioned the elephant in the room: the layoffs.
american.exampleSpanish: Nadie mencionó el elefante en la habitación: los despidos.

american.meaning: very rarely
american.verificationNote: DLE: higo, loc. adv. coloq., “Muy de tarde en tarde”
american.exampleEnglish: We see them once in a blue moon.
american.exampleSpanish: Los vemos de higos a brevas.

american.meaning: ease the first awkwardness between people so a conversation can start
american.verificationNote: DLE: hielo, loc. verb. coloq.
american.exampleEnglish: A joke helped break the ice at dinner.
american.exampleSpanish: Una broma sirvió para romper el hielo en la cena.

american.meaning: sense the mood
american.spanish: Captar el ambiente / saber interpretar el ambiente
american.verificationNote: Usage. Only a translators’ forum (ProZ) supports it, not a dictionary. “Tomar el pulso al ambiente” not found as a set phrase; “leer la sala” found in no source, so avoid it
american.exampleEnglish: Read the room before you pitch.
american.exampleSpanish: Capta el ambiente antes de presentar la propuesta.

american.english: It’s on me / I’ll pick up the tab
american.meaning: offering to pay for the meal or drinks yourself
american.spanish: Invito yo / esto corre por mi cuenta
american.verificationNote: Attested: SpanishDict, Gymglish (sources vary between “corre de / por / a mi cuenta”). Avoid “es en mí”
american.exampleEnglish: Put your wallet away, it’s on me.
american.exampleSpanish: Guarda la cartera, invito yo.

american.meaning: politely decline an invitation now, leaving open the chance of accepting another time
american.spanish: Lo dejamos para otro día / para otra ocasión
american.verificationNote: Gloss. Sense attested: WordReference, Larousse (“dejar para otra ocasión”). “Otra vez será” dropped: it can sound like a final refusal. Avoid “tomar un cheque de lluvia”
american.exampleEnglish: Can I take a rain check on dinner?
american.exampleSpanish: ¿Lo dejamos para otro día, lo de la cena?

american.meaning: a warning sign that something is wrong or risky
american.verificationNote: Attested: Fundéu RAE prefers “bandera roja” to the anglicism “red flag” (read via an EFE reprint, not on Fundéu’s own site)
american.exampleEnglish: He never lets her see friends: red flag.
american.exampleSpanish: No la deja ver a sus amigas: mala señal.

american.meaning: blame or sacrifice someone, often a colleague, to protect yourself or gain an advantage
american.spanish: Cargarle el muerto a alguien / echarle el muerto
american.verificationNote: DLE (partial): muerto, sense 7 “responsabilidad”, example “Me cargaron el muerto” (coloq.). Echar el muerto is not in the DLE but WordReference and SpanishDict list it. It means shifting blame, not betrayal
american.exampleEnglish: He threw his assistant under the bus.
american.exampleSpanish: Le cargó el muerto a su ayudante.

american.meaning: change the rules or targets partway through so that success becomes harder
american.verificationNote: Attested: PONS (colloquial), SpanishDict Answers (a contributor from Spain). It can also mean “be a game changer”, so context decides. “Mover los postes” found in no source
american.exampleEnglish: They keep moving the goalposts.
american.exampleSpanish: Siguen cambiando las reglas del juego.

american.meaning: a personal stake
american.spanish: Tener algo en juego (business) / jugarse el pellejo (stronger)
american.verificationNote: DLE (partial) for jugarse el pellejo: pellejo, loc. verb. coloq., “Arriesgar la vida”, so stronger than the English; Wiktionary agrees. Tener algo en juego is usage, with no source read
american.exampleEnglish: Investors need skin in the game.
american.exampleSpanish: Los inversores tienen que tener algo en juego.

american.english: Cost an arm and a leg
american.meaning: be extremely expensive
american.spanish: Costar un ojo de la cara / costar un riñón
american.verificationNote: Attested: SpanishDict (colloquial); RAE Diccionario del estudiante uses “te va a costar un ojo de la cara”. Costar un riñón entered the DRAE in 2010 (Telemetro)
american.exampleEnglish: That watch costs an arm and a leg.
american.exampleSpanish: Ese reloj cuesta un ojo de la cara.

american.meaning: extremely cheap; a bargain price
american.verificationNote: DLE: tirado, “Que se da muy barata o es de fácil realización”
american.exampleEnglish: Flights to Lisbon are dirt cheap.
american.exampleSpanish: Los vuelos a Lisboa están tirados.

american.meaning: a rough estimate, close enough but not exact
american.spanish: Una cifra aproximada / a ojo de buen cubero
american.verificationNote: Attested: Larousse (“ball-park figure” → cifra aproximada, informal); WordReference (a ojo de buen cubero, “sin medida, a bulto”). The second is an adverbial phrase and folksy for business
american.exampleEnglish: Give me a ballpark figure.
american.exampleSpanish: Dame una cifra aproximada.

american.meaning: the plan has failed, so you have to start again from scratch
american.spanish: Volver a la casilla de salida / volver a empezar desde cero
american.verificationNote: Attested: SpanishDict, Larousse. Casilla de salida is closer to “back to square one”. The DLE casilla page lacks the phrase. Avoid “volver a la mesa de dibujo”
american.exampleEnglish: The client rejected it; back to the drawing board.
american.exampleSpanish: El cliente lo rechazó: volvemos a la casilla de salida.

american.meaning: something very easy to do
american.verificationNote: DLE: pan, “ser algo pan comido”, loc. verb. coloq., “Ser muy fácil de conseguir”
american.exampleEnglish: The renewal was a piece of cake.
american.exampleSpanish: Renovar el contrato fue pan comido.

american.meaning: wait until the next day to decide, so you have time to think it over
american.verificationNote: DLE: almohada, “aconsejarse, o consultar, con la almohada”, locs. verbs. coloqs.
american.exampleEnglish: I’ll sleep on it.
american.exampleSpanish: Lo consulto con la almohada y te digo algo mañana.

american.meaning: become nervous or doubtful about a plan and want to back out
american.verificationNote: Attested: SpanishDict, Larousse (“se echó atrás”), WordReference (rajarse, coloq.). Entrarle canguelo means getting scared, not necessarily backing out. Avoid “pies fríos”
american.exampleEnglish: He got cold feet before the wedding.
american.exampleSpanish: Se echó atrás antes de la boda.

american.meaning: accept and get on with something unpleasant that cannot be avoided
american.verificationNote: DLE: tripa, loc. verb. coloq., “Esforzarse para disimular el miedo, dominarse”. Close in sense, not identical
american.exampleEnglish: I bit the bullet and called the notary.
american.exampleSpanish: Hice de tripas corazón y llamé al notario.

american.meaning: reduce the risk of loss by covering more than one outcome
american.spanish: Nadar y guardar la ropa / cubrirse las espaldas
american.verificationNote: Attested in learner sources only (Inklingo, Speaking Latino); Larousse gives “cubrirse, guardarse las espaldas”. No DLE page read
american.exampleEnglish: He’s hedging his bets with two offers.
american.exampleSpanish: Quiere nadar y guardar la ropa con dos ofertas.

canadian.meaning: go all out; also “party hard” (a Western Canadian sense)
canadian.verificationNote: Gloss. English: DCHP labels the “party hard” sense Western Canada, informal. DLE: resto, “echar el resto”, coloq., “Hacer todo el esfuerzo posible”; SpanishDict for darlo todo. Spanish loses the rural, beer-and-work flavour
canadian.exampleSpanish: Lo dimos todo el fin de semana.

canadian.verificationNote: Gloss. English confirmed (DCHP, “Cdn informal”). Two Spanish ideas in one: SpanishDict, empollón (coloq., pejorative, Spain); Larousse, pelota (pejorative, a flatterer). Neither is an exact match
canadian.exampleEnglish: The new hire is a total keener.
canadian.exampleSpanish: El nuevo es un pelota: siempre se ofrece para todo.

canadian.verificationNote: DLE: circo, sense 9, coloq., “Confusión, desorden, caos”. Larousse for desmadre (familiar); the DLE page for it would not load. English: DCHP and Wiktionary (Canada); it comes from a US TV show. Circo suits a farce, desmadre wild chaos
canadian.exampleEnglish: The meeting was a gong show.

canadian.verificationNote: Gloss. English: Dictionary.com, “Canadian slang”, but derogatory and dated, so teach it for recognition only. SpanishDict: cenutrio, colloquial, Spain, “twit”. Pardillo means gullible, not goofy
Attested: Castellano Actual (Universidad de Piura) lists ¿no?, ¿verdad? and ¿eh? as confirmatory tags. English: Merriam-Webster, “used especially in Canadian English”. Spanish ¿eh? can sound abrupt

Usage. Canadian reflex apology is cultural lore, not a dictionary label. Inklingo: perdón = “Excuse me. / Sorry.” Con permiso (DLE permiso, courtesy formula) is polite, but I could not verify how usual it is in Spain
canadian.exampleEnglish: Sorry, can I just squeeze by?

canadian.verificationNote: Usage. Canadian by habit, not by dictionary. No Spanish source read; the understatement works the same way in Spain

canadian.english: Take a kick at the can
canadian.verificationNote: Attested: SpanishDict (probar suerte, “to try one’s luck”). English: Wiktionary, “chiefly US and Canada”; no Canadian dictionary label found
canadian.exampleEnglish: I’ll take a kick at the can.

canadian.verificationNote: DLE: jaleo (coloq.) “Alboroto, tumulto, pendencia”; follón (coloq.) “Alboroto, discusión tumultuosa”. English: Merriam-Webster; the Canadian Oxford Dictionary (COD-2) marks it “Cdn, Brit., & Austral. informal” (as cited in DCHP, which says it “appears to be a Canadianism in the North American context”), so it is shared with British and Australian English

canadian.meaning: help with a shared task, or contribute money
canadian.spanish: Echar una mano / arrimar el hombro
canadian.verificationNote: Attested: SpanishDict (colloquial). Arrimar el hombro suggests a heavier shared effort. The DLE hombro page would not load. English: Dictionary.com; not Canadian-labelled

canadian.meaning: going to a vacation home, usually by a lake
canadian.spanish: Ir a la casa de campo / a la casa del lago
canadian.verificationNote: Gloss. English: DCHP, “cottage country”, chiefly Ontario and Manitoba (COD-2 “Cdn”). Avoid “casa rural”, which in Spain means a rental lodging
canadian.exampleEnglish: We’re going up to the cottage.
canadian.exampleSpanish: Nos vamos a la casa de campo.

canadian.meaning: a person, often retired, who spends winter somewhere warm (for Canadians, usually the southern US)
canadian.spanish: Residente de invierno / persona que pasa el invierno en el sur (a menudo jubilada)
canadian.verificationNote: Gloss. English confirmed (DCHP). Residentes de invierno is attested in Spain’s press (Alicante Plaza), but no single established word exists. Invernante is a bird term. Avoid “pájaro de nieve”
canadian.exampleSpanish: Nuestros vecinos son residentes de invierno.

canadian.meaning: the electricity bill (in Canada, 'hydro' means electricity)
canadian.verificationNote: Attested: OCU uses factura de la luz as its standard term. English: DCHP, sense 2, “Electricity supplied as a utility” (COD-2 “Cdn”). Warn learners that hidro- suggests water in Spain
canadian.exampleSpanish: La factura de la luz es altísima.

canadian.spanish: La moneda de un dólar (la del colimbo) / la de dos dólares
canadian.verificationNote: Gloss. English: Merriam-Webster, toonie “Canada, informal”; Oxford Learner’s tags loonie Canadian. The loon is colimbo grande (CMS; Birds of the World), not somormujo, which is a grebe in Spain (MITECO). Do not use duro or peseta
canadian.exampleSpanish: Es la moneda canadiense de dos dólares.

canadian.meaning: an older Canadian word for a sofa; most people now say “couch”
canadian.verificationNote: Usage. English: Dictionary.com, “Chiefly Canadian”. Plain sofá is right for that sense; sofá Chester (Divinity, Idealista) is only the tufted leather style

canadian.spanish: Gorro de lana / gorro de punto
canadian.verificationNote: DLE: gorro, “Pieza redonda, de tela o de punto, para cubrir y abrigar la cabeza”. SpanishDict: gorro de lana, “wool hat”, “beanie”. English: Dictionary.com, “in Canada, a knitted winter cap”. Avoid gorra, a peaked cap, and toca, a different object

canadian.meaning: a public toilet or restroom (Canadian usage)
canadian.verificationNote: Attested: SpanishDict, aseos tagged as used in Spain. English confirmed (DCHP, “esp. Cdn.”). Use baño at home

canadian.spanish: Una tienda de alimentación / una tienda de barrio abierta hasta tarde
canadian.verificationNote: Gloss. English: Dictionary.com, “(in Quebec)”; effectively Quebec only. Larousse: convenience store = “tienda de ultramarinos (que abre hasta tarde)”. DLE: colmado, “Tienda de comestibles”, but regional. No exact equivalent
canadian.exampleSpanish: Voy un momento a la tienda de la esquina.

canadian.spanish: Triturador de basura / triturador de residuos
canadian.verificationNote: Attested: WordReference (“garbage disposal”). English confirmed: DCHP (OED-3 “Chiefly Canad.”, COD-2 “Cdn.”). Rare in Spanish kitchens, so learners may need to explain it
canadian.exampleSpanish: El triturador de basura está atascado.

canadian.verificationNote: Attested: WordReference (canalón, canaleta, both tagged Spain). English: DCHP, COD-2 “N. Amer. (esp. Cdn)”. DCHP’s usage note says: “Eavestrough is virtually unknown outside Canada, and it is 25 times more common in Canadian English than in American English” (see its Chart 1). So it is much more prevalent in Canada, with only limited US use: DARE, as cited by DCHP, places that use “chiefly in the dialects of the northern and north midland US, and less often in the west”

canadian.meaning: coffee with two creams, two sugars
canadian.spanish: Un café con dos de leche y dos de azúcar
canadian.verificationNote: Gloss. English: DCHP, “a cup of coffee with two servings of cream and sugar” (COD-2 “Cdn”); tied to Tim Hortons. DLE defines café cortado as “café con muy poca leche”, so do not render it as cortado
canadian.exampleSpanish: Un café con dos de leche y dos de azúcar, por favor.

canadian.verificationNote: Gloss. English: DCHP, COD-2 “Cdn informal”. Spain has no nickname for it
canadian.exampleEnglish: Bring a two-four to the cottage.
canadian.exampleSpanish: Trae una caja de 24 cervezas a la casa de campo.

canadian.meaning: a 375 ml flat bottle of liquor
canadian.verificationNote: DLE: petaca, sense 3, “Botella de bolsillo, ancha y plana”; WordReference, “hip flask”. A Spanish petaca is usually smaller than 375 ml, so media botella is more accurate. English: DCHP gives it as slang only, with no modern dictionary label
canadian.exampleEnglish: He had a mickey in his jacket.
canadian.exampleSpanish: Llevaba una petaca en la chaqueta.

canadian.verificationNote: Attested: HyperDic (refresco, “pop, soda”). English: DCHP, “most common generic term” in Canada outside Quebec, but also used in the US Midwest. DLE gaseosa names one specific fizzy lemonade in Spain, so avoid it as the generic

Gloss. DLE: vaquero, “Hecho con tela vaquera”. Spanish press: The Objective (“total looks vaqueros”), El Corte Inglés (“doble denim”). English: DCHP records it (“a combination of blue jeans and denim jacket”, informal, at times jocular; earliest quotation 2002; “seems to originate in Canada around the year 2000”). Dictionary.com labels it “American” and facetious and says “First recorded in 1995–2000”, so it is a recent term with no Canadian label in Dictionary.com. The joke needs explaining: “el esmoquin canadiense, o sea, vaquero con vaquero”
canadian.exampleEnglish: He showed up in a Canadian tuxedo.
canadian.exampleSpanish: Apareció con un total look vaquero.

statusDefinitions.definition: the exact Spanish phrase was read on dle.rae.es in this check, with its marking (coloq., loc. verb.). “DLE (partial)” means only a related sense or example was read.
not confirmed in the DLE here, but listed in a bilingual dictionary (SpanishDict, WordReference, Larousse), Wiktionary or Spain-based press. Named in the status cell.
natural Peninsular Spanish from my own knowledge; no source I could read confirmed it. Check before you publish it as verified.
Spanish has no fixed idiom, so the rendering explains the meaning rather than translating the phrase.
a literal calque that people in Spain would not say; shown so learners recognise the trap.

verificationNotes.overview: No entry is checked against the RAE alone: where a DLE page would not load, the rendering was tested against bilingual dictionaries, Fundéu, Spain-based press and, for the English side, the Dictionary of Canadianisms (DCHP) and other dictionaries.

manualChecks.heading: Check by hand on dle.rae.es before you print “verified”.
manualChecks.text: These DLE pages would not load, so the entries rest on other sources: grano, rama, ojo, rajar, hombro, nadar, pulso and the noun desmadre. Four entries are still tagged Usage, with no source read: read the room, sorry, not bad and chesterfield. The “tener algo en juego” half of skin in the game is also unsourced.

“Echar el muerto” is not in the DLE; only “cargar el muerto” is, as an example under muerto.
The loon on the dollar coin is colimbo grande, not somormujo (a grebe in Spain).

sourceLimitations.heading: How far to trust the sources.
sourceLimitations.text: SpanishDict, WordReference and Larousse show that a phrase is in use, not that the RAE endorses it, and SpanishDict’s regional tags are sometimes wrong. Fundéu’s preference for “bandera roja” was read through an EFE reprint, not on Fundéu’s own site. Pages were read through a summarising fetch tool, so quotes are as it reported them.

sourceDocument.title: Verb Wise: North American Expressions Collection

audienceAndMethod.heading: Audience and method
paragraphs: Each of the 50 expressions below carries a status tag showing how far its Spanish rendering was checked against the RAE's Diccionario de la lengua española (DLE) and, where the DLE page would not load, against bilingual dictionaries and Spain-based press, because the RAE site was only partly reachable.

The collection is aimed at English-speaking adults aged 35–55 with the means and flexibility to move abroad: remote workers, business owners, established professionals and early retirees. They already speak capable English, so the focus is on the finer points of Spanish: humour and sarcasm, social situations, money and work, and decisions and risk. The 25 British sayings stay as their own collection.

american.heading: American collection (25)
american.text: These 25 expressions are grouped by the situations an American adult in Spain actually meets them in. 7 have a full DLE reading, 2 a partial one, 14 are attested in other sources, 1 is a gloss and 1 is natural usage still to confirm. Many are shared with Canadian English; the Canadian section covers the distinctly Canadian ones.

canadian.heading: Canadian collection (25)
canadian.text: These 25 are distinctly Canadian, or used in Canada in ways a Spanish speaker will not expect, so many have no Spanish idiom and need a short gloss. A dictionary labels 18 of them Canadian: keener, snowbird, washroom, give’r (only its “party hard” sense carries a regional label, Western Canada), gong show, double-double, loonie and toonie, toque, cottage country, hydro, chesterfield, two-four, eh, hoser, dépanneur, garburator, eavestrough and kerfuffle (Canadian Oxford Dictionary “Cdn, Brit., & Austral. informal”, as cited by the Dictionary of Canadianisms). The other 7 are Canadian by usage or stereotype, with no Canadian dictionary label found: pitch in, not bad, sorry, Canadian tuxedo (the Dictionary of Canadianisms records it as emerging in Canada around 2000, but Dictionary.com labels it American), mickey, pop and take a kick at the can. “Hang a Larry” was dropped because the Dictionary of Canadianisms defines it as a left turn, not a U-turn, and “beauty!” because no dictionary labels it Canadian.

conversionNotes: The fields version, description, language, targetDialect and the top-level categories structure were supplied by the converter; all other text comes from the source document.

The English cell of each source table row was split at its final parenthetical: the text before it is english and the text inside it is meaning. Where the source row has no parenthetical, meaning is null because the source gives no separate meaning.
status holds the label that opens the source status cell; verificationNote holds the whole source status cell. No label was upgraded or changed.

Markdown emphasis markers (asterisks) and link syntax were removed; all other characters, including quotation marks, accents and punctuation, are unchanged. Example sentences keep their inner punctuation; only the outer quotation marks and the arrow separator were removed.
category ids are lowercase snake_case derived from the source section headings with the word "and" removed; the original headings are in categories.
The sources listed in sourcesRead are as stated in the source document. None was re-checked or independently verified during conversion.

meaningAdditions.note: The source document gave no separate meaning for these 19 American rows (meaning was null in the first conversion). The meanings were written afterwards in plain English from dictionary definitions, aligned to the sense of the paired Spanish equivalent. No other field of any record was changed.
meaningAdditions.sourceStatus: Definitions were read through a web-fetch summariser, not as raw page text, and were not re-checked against the raw pages. Meanings are paraphrased, not quoted.

entries.meaning: get straight to the main point, skipping the preamble
avoid the main point by talking around it, usually out of reluctance
entries.caveat: Fits andar con rodeos (evasive) best; andarse por las ramas can also mean simply rambling.

entries.english: Hit the nail on the head
entries.meaning: say or do exactly the right thing; be precisely right
an obvious major problem that everyone avoids mentioning
ease the first awkwardness between people so a conversation can start
entries.caveat: Merriam-Webster also lists the broader sense 'make a beginning'; the social sense is the one used here.

entries.english: It’s on me / I’ll pick up the tab
entries.meaning: offering to pay for the meal or drinks yourself
entries.caveat: Only 'pick up the tab' has a dictionary entry (labelled US, informal). 'It's on me' has no entry of its own; Oxford Learner's Dictionaries (US) shows it only as an example under 'on' (sense 14, 'paid for by'): 'Drinks are on me (= I am paying)', https://www.oxfordlearnersdictionaries.com/us/definition/english/on (read through a web-fetch summary). So that half of the meaning is supported by one dictionary example and common usage, not by a headword.

entries.meaning: politely decline an invitation now, leaving open the chance of accepting another time
entries.caveat: Noun 'rain check' also means a ticket or voucher for a later date; that sense is not the one used here. Said by the person declining, whereas the Spanish equivalent is more neutral.

entries.meaning: blame or sacrifice someone, often a colleague, to protect yourself or gain an advantage
entries.caveat: English also covers criticising someone publicly; cargarle el muerto is narrower (shifting blame or burden).

entries.meaning: change the rules or targets partway through so that success becomes harder
